It's weekly movie night. You and the gang select this film because it seems like a wholesome found-family black comedy. It begins swimmingly; the guts, gore, and over-the-top acting make for interesting composition. Young Natalie Portman is acting her heart out. The contrasting dynamics: young and old, vengeance and reluctance, adopted daughter and father, are excellent narrative elements certain to yield a 4 star rating. Wait. Why do they keep flirting with each other. Cut that out. And so you watch in horror as the film all but decides to pursue a forbidden romance between a twelve-year-old and a guy who's the same age as George Bush. Scenes you can scarcely describe, but were somehow approved by a movie studio, are horrifically plastered across the screen. You forget this was suppose to be a buddy assassin story. You spiral into utter despair knowing that a child actress was involved in this. The story crescendos in spite of narrative whiplash, and soon the denouement crashes down upon us. The camerawork and tension, elegantly scripted, work in tandem to effectuate stunning fight choreography. A satisfying and bittersweet ending has Leon, in his insistence to not sully Mathilda's soul, grant the long-awaited revenge on her behalf. It's a beautifully written and directed scene, which only begs the question, why didn't they just do more of this then??? The most frustrating part is that the potential of this movie, where tumultuous character exploration brings about themes of absolution and salvation, becomes the background in entertaining the fetishization of abuse. It takes an otherwise intriguing, darkly comedic premise and ruins it because the director wanted to flaunt how much he likes kids (not an allegation - legally verified). You cannot separate art from the artist when the artist genuinely makes his pedophilic nature the audience's problem.

Him telling Mathilda to stop talking to another boy around her age “to protect her” while the scene is cinematically imply it as an act of jealousy, is particularly disturbing. The restaurant scene, sick! The creepy camera angles and directing choices make the whole thing feel deeply uncomfortable. The movie promises a 10/10 experience, but ends up showing us creepy directing. My problem isn’t necessarily with exploring a child’s premature understanding of maturity and intimacy under her circumstances. My issue is with how the director chooses to portray it. It’s extremely weird, unjustified, and ruins the movie for me. From the romantic musical cues during their embraces to the conversations about love and sexual attraction, the film repeatedly borrows the language of cinematic romance to frame a relationship between a 12-year-old girl and an adult man. Even the scenes where they share a bed become difficult to interpret independently because of the conversation they had just ten minutes earlier. And the fact that Natalie Portman was only 12 during filming makes these directorial choices even more disturbing. There's something deeply uncomfortable about the creative decisions the adults behind this movie made. It’s Lolita as an action movie, except that, unlike Lolita, this one doesn’t meaningfully criminalise or challenge the behaviour it puts on screen. These creepy directorial choices really ruined what could have been a great movie for me.

I had A LOT of questions watching this film, most still unanswered. The premise of the story if not weird is at the very least peculiar. An assassin who runs into a little girl after her family is killed, embraces her and trains her upon her insisting. Then develops a romantic relationship after she falls in love with her, all the while denying it. Finally he dies while avenging her. Now I KNOW this is a fraction of what the movie was but still. Why was I told this story. Why would I care about Leon, just because his life is shown to be tragic and lonely and most of what  we know about him has been shown through exposition. As far as Mathillda Natalie Portman's character is concerned, it was played exceptionally, but what the hell was that? Why would a 13 year old behave in such a manner, because of her abusive past, traumatic experiences? What made her mature the way she did? Is it ever possible for someone to be like that, and if so what does it signify? Her maturity seems like a lazy excuse for the sexualization of a child. Her carrying a stuffed toy throughout the film, symbolizing her still being innocent is odd af. You know why? A kid should not need anything to show their innocence, but because of the weird and ample sexual innuendos the character is forced into it was somehow required. Gary Oldman being the central villain playing a deranged corrupt cop who kills as he pleases was kinda cool. But again why would I give a shit if the violence is just there to show how intense he is which is sad because he is supposed be the focal point, representing the city and its dystopian, run down, gritty and evil nature. Leon's handler, is also the guy who raised him after he fled from Italy and came to the US and throughout the film, he is shown as an ambiguous guy who is exploiting Leon sorta but in a way is also is his father figure, whom he also respects and trust as we say when he introduces Mathilda or entrusts him with her if anything were to happen to him. In the final scenes we say how he was somewhat distraught from Leon's death and he was sincere in that as he did not want the same for Mathilda. All these characters symbolized something but exactly what? What was the film trying to convey and how did they all tie in? This is exactly why the ending, although somewhat the highlight of the film, leaves me apathetic to it all. At a surface level this film is a pedophilic fantasy and because it has no real depth, it just looks like its trying really hard to prove itself as being something otherwise. Well, it turns out the director groomed a girl starting at age 12 and impregnated her when she was 15, which is the minimum age of consent in France. Oh well, I can separate art from artist. I went into this movie in 2026 fully willing to go to bat for it and continue to love it despite how badly its reputation has suffered in the last decade. “Is life always this hard, or is it just when you’re a kid?” Léon: O Profissional é um filme que me surpreendeu por conseguir encontrar sensibilidade em meio a uma narrativa extremamente violenta. Por trás de sua história de vingança, brutalidade e ação, existe um retrato inesperadamente delicado sobre solidão, afeto e duas pessoas que, por caminhos completamente diferentes, acabam encontrando uma na outra algo que parecia faltar em suas vidas. Acompanhamos Léon, um assassino profissional que leva uma vida solitária em Nova York, seguindo uma rotina rigorosa e mantendo pouquíssimos vínculos com o mundo exterior. Sua existência muda quando conhece Mathilda, uma garota de doze anos cuja família é assassinada por um grupo de policiais corruptos liderados pelo imprevisível Norman Stansfield. Depois de escapar do massacre, ela encontra abrigo no apartamento de Léon, dando início a uma convivência que transforma profundamente a vida dos dois. A atuação de Jean Reno como Léon é impressionante. Seu personagem é um homem de poucas palavras, extremamente disciplinado e aparentemente incapaz de demonstrar sentimentos, mas que revela uma humanidade enorme nos pequenos gestos. Por trás de sua aparência intimidadora, há um homem ingênuo em diversos aspectos da vida cotidiana, não sabendo ler nem escrever, que aparece ter aprendido a sobreviver sem nunca ter realmente descoberto como viver. Natalie Portman é a minha atriz favorita, e ver a sua estreia no cinema foi bem especial para mim. Mesmo em uma personagem de tamanha complexidade, marcada por experiências traumáticas, que tenta encontrar alguma estabilidade em um mundo que lhe tirou praticamente tudo. Natalie Portman demonstra uma maturidade impressionante, conseguindo transmitir a revolta, a vulnerabilidade e a determinação da personagem. Sua presença é fundamental para que a história funcione, especialmente porque é através dela que começamos a enxergar Léon de uma maneira diferente. A relação entre os dois é, sem dúvidas, o aspecto mais interessante do filme. O que começa como uma convivência improvável se transforma em um vínculo de confiança, proteção e companheirismo. Mathilda apresenta a Léon um mundo que ele nunca teve oportunidade de conhecer, enquanto ele oferece a ela um tipo de segurança que parecia impossível encontrar. Gary Oldman, por sua vez, constrói um antagonista verdadeiramente perturbador. Seu Norman Stansfield é imprevisível, exagerado e assustadoramente instável. Cada aparição traz uma sensação de desconforto, e Oldman aproveita essa liberdade para entregar uma atuação memorável. O personagem funciona como uma presença ameaçadora constante, contrastando diretamente com a aparente tranquilidade de Léon. Tecnicamente, Luc Besson demonstra bastante personalidade na condução da narrativa. A fotografia explora a atmosfera urbana de Nova York, enquanto a montagem alterna momentos de ação intensa com cenas mais contemplativas. A trilha sonora de Éric Serra também merece atenção, contribuindo para a identidade do filme e reforçando tanto sua tensão quanto sua melancolia. Mesmo nas sequências mais violentas, existe uma preocupação em preservar o lado humano da história. É importante reconhecer que o filme também apresenta algumas escolhas narrativas desconfortáveis, especialmente na maneira como aborda a relação de Mathilda com Léon. A personagem expressa sentimentos que ultrapassam o companheirismo, e essa dimensão exige uma leitura cuidadosa. Ainda assim, acredito que a força da obra está na construção de um vínculo que, em seu aspecto mais profundo, fala sobre cuidado, confiança e a possibilidade de encontrar uma família onde menos se espera. Léon: O Profissional é muito mais do que um filme sobre um assassino e uma garota em busca de vingança. É uma história sobre pessoas que aprenderam a viver isoladas e que, por acaso, encontram uma razão para olhar além de suas próprias circunstâncias. Existe uma tristeza muito particular nessa relação, mas também uma beleza enorme na maneira como ela transforma os dois personagens. Ao final, fica a sensação de que, mesmo em um mundo tão cruel, ainda é possível encontrar alguém que faça a vida parecer um pouco menos solitária.

There’s something deeply touching about the way Léon takes care of his plant. In a world where he struggles to connect with anyone, the plant is the closest thing he has to a home. He looks after it, cleans its leaves, waters it, and carries it with him wherever he goes. His line about loving the plant because it’s always happy and never asks questions says more about him than any monologue could. Behind the professional hitman is a lonely man who needs something to care for just as much as he needs someone to care for him. A small detail that becomes one of the film’s most meaningful symbols.
